name: Gareth Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a press line at Corbett Pressings. We stamp metal brackets and hinges for car seats and doors. It's four days on, four off, twelve hours, six till six. I start by checking the die is seated right, run the first parts and put them on the gauge before the line goes. After that it's feeding coil, watching for splits, clearing jams and keeping the bins moving so the forklift drivers aren't waiting on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm of a 400-tonne press when it's running sweet, honestly. I like Dave Kowalski, my shift lead, who's been there thirty years and can hear a die cracking before it shows. What wears me out is the night block in winter and the overtime going up and down with the car orders. Last spring we had three weeks of short time after Corbett lost a contract, and we had to dip into our savings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hannah is a dental nurse. We rent a two-bed flat on Mill Road, ten minutes from the plant. We've got about three months of bills put away and we're building a house deposit, slowly. My mum and dad live five minutes away and we're there every Sunday for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds a lot like now, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly. At break the lads talk about robots taking over every few months, and nothing ever happens at our place. Online I wouldn't bother, I only post about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my worry, the order book is. If Corbett loses another car contract, we go back on short time whether there's AI or not. The office might use it for scheduling, which is fine by me if the rota stops changing at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up and take the overtime when it's going. Hannah and I would keep putting 200 a month in the house fund and leave the three months of bills untouched. I've been meaning to ask about the setter course, the people who change the dies, so I'd probably finally do it, because setters get kept on when it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, but not relaxed. Short time last spring still sits with me. A normal year for us still has a wobble in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said setters get kept on when it's quiet. Who goes first if the orders drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agency staff first, then the newer operators. I'm in the middle, five years in, so not first but not safe either. Marek, the setter I eat lunch with, says setters never get laid off because nobody else can change a die in under an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If short time came again, what gets cut at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday goes first, we'd planned a week by the sea in June. Then takeaways and my gym membership. The house fund would stop, which is the bit that really stings, because every month we stop saving is another month paying someone else's mortgage.

say: I'd tell the lads at break that the **robot scare** came to nothing, like I always said.
I'd keep it **offline**, because I only post about football.
think: My real worry is the **order book**, since one lost car contract means short time.
Office **scheduling software** is fine by me if it stops the rota changing at midnight.
do: Keep taking **overtime** whenever Corbett offers it.
Keep putting **200 a month** into the house fund and leave the bills money alone.
Sign up for the **setter course**, because setters are kept on when work is quiet.
feel: I feel fairly **settled**, but last spring's **short time** still sits with me.
S0.quote: Every month we stop saving is another month paying someone else's mortgage.
fieldNote: His worry in a flat world is **car orders**, rooted in real short time last spring.
He sees the **setter course** as job insurance more than ambition.
The **house fund** matters most to him; pausing it hurts more than losing the holiday.

steps.text: Keep working the four-on four-off press shifts and take overtime
Pay 200 a month into the house deposit fund with Hannah
Ask Dave about the setter course and enrol this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one sounds more like where things are heading, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what my dad used to say, that machines come and you change with them. I'd probably say it louder than I believe it. Online I might share something about apprenticeships, because that's the bit everyone forgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the office gets it first, the planners and the buyers, and we'd see fewer of them. On the floor, Corbett would put a robot arm on the unload end of my press, because that's the easy bit, picking a bracket off a belt. Then I'm minding two presses instead of one, and they need half the operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the setter course for definite, and I'd ask to be on whatever robot cell they put in first, because whoever learns it first keeps a job. I'd use the AI on my phone a bit more, to explain the robot manuals in plain words. We'd push the house fund up to 300 a month and hold off on the newer car Hannah's been wanting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared yet. It's a few years off on the floor, and I can see it coming, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd need half the operators. Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave mostly. He's 58, brilliant with his ears and hands, but he won't touch a tablet. If they pushed him out two years before his pension, that'd be wrong, and I'd tell the manager so even if it didn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say it louder than you believe it. What's the gap there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap is simple. I'd tell everyone you change with the machines, but I've had one press job since college and never changed with anything. I believe it's right for the country, I'm just not sure I'm the one who'll do it well.

say: I'd repeat my dad's line at work that **machines come** and you change with them.
Online I'd share something about **apprenticeships**, because everyone forgets the training side.
think: The **office staff** feel it first, and the floor follows when Corbett buys a robot arm.
A robot on the **unload end** means minding two presses, so they'd need half the operators.
do: Finish the **setter course** and volunteer for the first robot cell Corbett installs.
Use the **phone AI** to explain the robot manuals in plain words.
Raise the house fund to **300 a month** and put off Hannah's newer car.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but not scared, because the floor change is still **a few years** away.
S1.quote: I'd tell everyone you change with the machines, but I've had one press job since college and never changed with anything.
fieldNote: He expects the operator team to **halve**, which puts his own place in question.
There's an honest gap between his public **change-with-it line** and his record of never changing.
His concern for **Dave**, close to his pension, shows a strong sense of loyalty and fairness.

steps.text: Finish the setter course and volunteer for Corbett's first robot cell
Use the phone chatbot to explain the robot cell manuals
Raise the house deposit savings to 300 a month
Put off buying Hannah a newer car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different thing altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say keep calm, it's the office jobs that go first and people like us still have a few years. I'd say it on the shift group chat to stop the panic, because some of the younger agency lads would be walking out the gate by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be counting. AGI in 2028 means the planners and buyers at Corbett are gone straight away. Robots on the floor by 2031 means I'd be 32 with no job and a skill nobody needs. Three extra years is not long when you've only ever stood at a press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into a proper trade straight away, maybe maintenance electrician, because somebody has to fix the robots for a while. I'd ask Corbett to sponsor the apprenticeship and do nights at college if they won't. We'd stop the house hunt and keep the deposit as a cushion. I'd also talk to my dad, because he went through the steelworks closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick. Not panicked, because there's still those three years on the floor, but it'd be on my mind every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for your actual day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years nothing changes at the press, but the schedule, the orders and the quality reports all come from a computer. Then by 2031 the press doesn't need me. So the gap is my window to get a ticket in something else, and I'd treat it like a countdown clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not buying a house yet, and that I'm sorry, because I promised her one by thirty. She'd be fine, she's tougher than me. Her job's safer than mine in that world anyway, nobody wants a robot in their mouth.

say: I'd tell the **group chat** to keep calm, because office jobs go first.
I'd try to stop the **agency lads** walking out the gate in a panic.
think: Corbett's **planners and buyers** would go at once, and the press floor by 2031.
I'd be **32** with no job and a skill nobody needs.
do: Start a **maintenance electrician** apprenticeship now, sponsored by Corbett or at night college.
**Pause the house hunt** and keep the deposit as an emergency cushion.
Talk to **my dad**, who lived through the steelworks closing.
feel: I feel a bit **sick**, though the three-year **robot gap** stops it becoming panic.
S2.quote: Robots on the floor by 2031 means I'd be 32 with no job and a skill nobody needs.
fieldNote: He treats the **three-year gap** as a countdown to get a trade qualification.
He's calming in public but privately **counting years**, a clear gap between say and think.
Breaking his **house promise** to Hannah is the most personal cost he names.

steps.text: Start a maintenance electrician apprenticeship, at Corbett or night college
Pause the house hunt with Hannah and hold the deposit
Ask Dad how he got through the steelworks closing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it, if it has to happen at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where we've got no excuse. Five years is enough to get a trade, and I'd say that to the younger lads and to my cousin who's just started at Corbett. I'd say the government should put money into apprenticeships now instead of handouts after the fact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, robots by 2034 gives me seven years at the press, and I'd be 34. That's enough to get the electrician qualification properly and work a couple of years at it. Whether electricians last after that, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the setter course and start electrical classes at night, two evenings a week. Hannah and I would still buy a home, but a smaller one, maybe a flat, so the mortgage could be paid on her wage alone. I'd build up six months of bills by 2030, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but in charge of it, if that makes sense. Five years feels like a plan, two years felt like a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mortgage would have to work on Hannah's wage alone. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because dental work is hands in mouths, and I don't see that going to a robot soon. If I'm the one retraining at 33, the house has to survive on her pay. My mum did the same when Dad was out of work, she kept us going on a school kitchen wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the thinking parts of your job, the planning and the paperwork, what changes when AGI arrives in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me, the planning is already done upstairs. My quality sheets would go on a tablet that checks itself, I suppose. The press itself is the job, so I'd watch the robot date, not the AGI date.

say: I'd tell the younger lads and **my cousin** that five years is enough to learn a trade.
I'd say government should fund **apprenticeships** now rather than handouts later.
think: Robots by **2034** give me seven more years at the press, until I'm 34.
I can't tell whether **electricians** will still be needed after the robots arrive.
do: Start **night classes** in electrical work two evenings a week, alongside the setter course.
Buy a **smaller home** whose mortgage Hannah's wage alone can cover.
Build savings to **six months** of bills by 2030.
feel: I feel **worried but in control**, because five years feels like a plan.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a plan, two years felt like a fire.
fieldNote: He watches the **robot date**, not the AGI date, since planning is already done upstairs.
He designs the **mortgage** around Hannah's safer job, echoing what his mother once did.
He backs **apprenticeships** over handouts, true to his traditional, free-market views.

steps.text: Take electrical night classes two evenings a week
Buy a smaller flat that Hannah's wage alone can cover
Build savings up to six months of bills by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth and last picture. This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 when the AI lands and 40 when the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, that's plenty of warning and nobody gets to moan later. I'd probably say it at Sunday dinner, and Dad would agree, he likes people standing on their own feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the dangerous one for me, because I'd put it off. I know myself. Ten years of warning would turn into ten years of saying I'll start the course after Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To beat that, I'd sign up for the setter course in the first month and tell Dave so he holds me to it. Meanwhile I'd keep running my press like normal. We'd buy the house in 2027 like we planned, and I'd aim to be a maintenance electrician by 2032, with a few years in before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, because I know I can be lazy about changing when nothing's on fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is dangerous because you'd put it off. Is that real, or a joke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real. When Corbett offered the setter course two years ago, I said I'd do it after Christmas, and I still haven't. That's why I'd tell Dave, he's the kind who asks every Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the family plans look like in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd do it the normal way. House, then wedding, then kids around thirty, with Mum and Dad down the road for babysitting. By the time robots come for the press, the kids would be at school and I'd hopefully be the one fixing the robots.

say: I'd say at **Sunday dinner** that ten years is plenty of warning.
I'd add that **nobody gets to moan** later, and Dad would agree.
think: Ten years is risky for me because I'd keep **putting it off**.
I already delayed the **setter course** two years ago and still haven't done it.
do: Enrol on the **setter course** in the first month and tell Dave to hold me to it.
Buy the **house in 2027** as planned and keep running the press as normal.
Aim to qualify as a **maintenance electrician** by 2032.
feel: I feel **mostly okay**, with a **nagging worry** that I'll get lazy when nothing's urgent.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning would turn into ten years of saying I'll start the course after Christmas.
fieldNote: His biggest risk in the long picture is his own **procrastination**, which he names honestly.
He uses **Dave** to keep himself accountable, trusting people more than plans.
Family plans keep a **traditional order**: house, then wedding, then children.

steps.text: Enrol on the setter course in month one and tell Dave
Buy the house in 2027, then plan the wedding
Keep running the press line at Corbett while studying

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. What would help is Corbett or the government paying for a real apprenticeship, with a wage while you train, not a six-week online course. I promised my partner Hannah a house by thirty, so I can't train for a new trade on no wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'd fix the robots. Somebody has to, at least at first, and it should be the people who know the presses. Give that work to people like Dave's crew before you hire someone from an agency who's never heard a die crack.

headlineQuote: I promised my partner Hannah a house by thirty, so I can't train for a new trade on no wage.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old press operator** at Corbett Pressings, renting a flat with Hannah, a dental nurse.
He has about **three months** saved and a slow-growing house fund he guards closely.
His traditional views favour **apprenticeships** and standing on your own feet over government handouts.
He's uneasy in the flat picture but turns **alarmed** when robots could reach the press by 2031.
Longer warnings suit him, though he admits he'd **procrastinate** with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because robots could take the press when he's only **32**.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship**, with a wage while training, funded by Corbett or government.
Giving **robot repair** work to experienced press workers before agency hires.
